paras: The expulsion of the Bushfield families from Vernon, Indiana, took place around October 22, 1903, when a mob ordered four families named Bushfield out of the Jennings County town and burned their four houses. The families were sent south and told not to return. Wire reports said the mob was believed to resent the light sentence a court had just given a Bushfield charged with attempted murder, and the item ran in papers from Georgia to North Dakota.

According to the dispatches, a man named Bushfield, called Leon, Len, Lon or Lew in different papers, had been charged with attempting to kill Frank Van Please on August 24. An Indianapolis dispatch said he pleaded guilty and received a jail sentence the day before the mob acted, while another version said his trial was held that week and that "his light sentence angered his neighbors." The Wilmington Evening Journal described the Bushfields as "colored"; the other reports found do not state their race.

Accounts of the hour differ: one wire version said the mob came "shortly after 9 o'clock at night," while others, dated October 22, said "early this morning" or "to-day." The mob marched to the four houses the Bushfield families occupied and ordered them to leave. After the families had moved their household goods into the street, they were ordered to go south, and they left in their wagons under orders not to return. The mob then set fire to the four houses, which were totally destroyed.

No report of arrests, an investigation or any official response appears in the coverage found, and no paper followed the families after they left. No paper named any member of the mob or gave its size.

The story moved as a short Associated Press item, credited as such in the Raleigh News & Observer, and ran from October 23 in papers in Delaware, Illinois, Minnesota, Georgia and Iowa. Weeklies in Wisconsin, Kansas, North Dakota and Indiana reprinted it through October 29, and the Minneapolis Journal reduced it to a single line in a news digest. The only Indiana paper found to carry it, the Plymouth Tribune, used the same wire text a week later.

Most papers printed the dispatch without comment and without mentioning race, presenting the mob's motive as a supposition. Headline writers framed it differently: the Wilmington Evening Journal used "Negroes Driven Out of Indiana Town," the Grant County Herald and the Plymouth Tribune "MORE INDIANA MOB LAW," and the Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican "Indianians Resent Court Sentence by Driving Out Four Families." The Savannah Morning News headed its version "ORDERED THEM SOUTH," adding that the mob "Drove the Bushfields in This Direction." No Black-press report of the expulsion was found.

The reports disagree on the timing, which fits either a night attack on October 21 or one early on October 22, and on whether Bushfield was tried or pleaded guilty. They agree that the sentence was light and came just before the mob acted.
